title: Roofing
headline: Roof structure, covering, fascia and gutters — the stage that keeps everything else dry.
seoTitle: Roofing in Nigeria: timber, long-span aluminium and stone-coated roofs explained
seoDescription: A guide to roof trusses, long-span aluminium and stone-coated sheets, gauges, fixings and fascia for Nigerian homes, with checks and photos to ask for.
summary: A good roof needs a strong, treated structure, the right sheet gauge and proper fixings. Leaks are expensive to chase later.
duration: 1–3 weeks depending on size and roof type [CHECK]
whatHappens: Roof structure: treated hardwood timber (commonly 2×4, 2×6 sizes) or steel trusses fixed to the wall plate with straps or bolts.
Purlins and noggins fixed across the rafters to carry the sheets.
Covering: long-span aluminium sheets (common gauges 0.45–0.55 mm) or stone-coated steel tiles, laid with the right overlap and roofing screws/nails with washers. [CHECK gauge on your specification]
Ridge capping, valleys, flashings where the roof meets walls, and fascia board.
Gutters and downpipes (if specified) leading rainwater away from the foundation.
problems: Untreated or wet timber — termites and warping later.
Thinner sheets supplied than paid for. Gauge is printed on many sheets; measure with a micrometer if in doubt.
Roof not tied down to the wall — risk of wind lifting it.
Too few purlins or screws, causing sagging sheets and leaks.
Poor flashing at valleys and parapets — the most common leak point.
Ceiling joists left out so the ceiling contractor later ‘needs extra timber’.
questions: What timber species and sizes are you using, and is it treated against termites?
What sheet gauge and brand, and can I see the label or delivery note?
How is the roof anchored to the walls?
What overlap and fixing spacing will you use?
How are valleys and wall junctions flashed?
photoCheckpoints: Timber on delivery and after treatment.
